slides.title: Identity choices depend on the current sample
body: **Identity matching** rewards selection of a comparison object with the same appearance as the sample. In the sea-lion preparation reviewed by Cook and colleagues, a central shape establishes the relation for that trial. The animal then selects the matching member of the side alternatives.

The sample changes which comparison is correct. A particular shape can serve as a sample, a matching choice or an alternative across different trials. Reinforcement follows the sample–comparison relation, requiring the animal to coordinate its inspection of the sample with its later selection.

The supplied Rio recording contains matching responses to the right and to the left on successive trials. These changes in response position retain the same identity rule. The publisher describes a tone followed by fish for correct choices, linking the selected relation to the trial consequence.

figure.caption: Cook et al. (2021), Fig. 17.2(a). Rocky in the sea-lion identity-matching preparation.

slides.title: Sea-lion brains connect sensory and motor regions
body: **Magnetic resonance imaging**, or MRI, distinguishes tissue within the sea-lion brain using signals generated in a magnetic field. Cook and colleagues present a structural view with extensive cortical folds and a prominent **caudate nucleus**, a subcortical structure involved in motor learning and reward.

**Gray matter** contains neuronal cell bodies and local processing networks, while **white matter** contains bundles of axons connecting regions. An axon conducts signals away from a neuron toward other cells. The structural image distinguishes cortical tissue from the connecting pathways beneath it.

**Diffusion tensor imaging** estimates directional water diffusion in tissue, allowing reconstruction of probable white-matter pathways. The published tractography identifies connections running along different anatomical axes. The **corpus callosum**, a white-matter structure crossing between the cerebral hemispheres, supplies routes through which processing in the two sides of the brain can interact.

figure.caption: Cook (2021), Fig. 17.3(a–c). Gross anatomy, structural MRI and diffusion tractography of sea-lion brains.

slides.title: More alternatives preserve the identity choice rule
body: Mauck and Dehnhardt trained a harbour seal to match physical objects, then increased the choice set from two alternatives to four. The sample specified which object was correct. Additional alternatives changed the selection demands while retaining identity as the rewarded relation.

The comparison objects were positioned around the sample, and the animal indicated its selection by touching an object with its snout. Correct matching earned reinforcement. The researchers varied the objects across successive problems, giving the same conditional choice requirement different physical materials.

The seal eventually selected matching objects from the larger comparison sets immediately upon introduction of unfamiliar objects. A successful choice required locating the sample’s counterpart among several alternatives. This performance extended the learned identity relation across both object sets and the number of available choices.

figure.caption: Mauck (2005), Fig. 1B. Novel objects used in identity-matching transfer.

slides.title: One-trial transfer requires choices before new feedback
body: **One-trial transfer** tests a learned relation with a problem presented only once. Mauck and Dehnhardt introduced new objects in the final transfer phase of their harbour-seal study. The animal selected among four comparisons, with the central sample specifying which object matched.

Earlier training had already varied stimulus sets and expanded the number of comparison alternatives. Performance developed across these successive problems, and the seal reached the matching criterion immediately with later unfamiliar object sets. Each change retained the relation between the sample and its identical comparison.

The seal matched correctly on 80% of the final one-trial problems. Each initial choice preceded reinforcement for that particular new problem. Successful performance therefore applied the previously acquired identity relation to the current objects at their first presentation.

figure.caption: Mauck (2005), Fig. 3. Acquisition and transfer across identity-matching problems.

slides.title: Same and different relations can guide distinct actions
body: **Same/different discrimination** classifies the relation between two stimuli. Scholtyssek and colleagues presented pairs of white shapes on a black monitor background to a harbour seal. The animal stayed at its station for identical pairs and moved toward the display for different pairs.

A **no-go response** means withholding the specified movement, while a **go response** means performing it. Here, both response types could be correct, depending on the displayed pair. The experimenter reinforced the response appropriate to that relation and changed the shapes across training problems.

Training progressed from repeated problems to problems presented only once. With trial-unique pairs, the seal responded correctly to unfamiliar same and different relations. The choice of action was governed by the relation within the pair, while the particular shape identities changed across problems.

figure.caption: Scholtyssek (2013), Fig. 2. Shape, brightness and pattern problems in the same/different task.

refs: Scholtyssek Christine, Kelber Almut, Hanke Frederike D., Dehnhardt Guido (2013). A harbor seal can transfer the same/different concept to new stimulus dimensions. Animal Cognition 16(6):915-925. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10071-013-0624-0

slides.title: Relational learning transfers across visual dimensions
body: After learning same/different judgments with shapes, the harbour seal in Scholtyssek and colleagues’ study encountered problems defined by **brightness** and **pattern**. Brightness concerns how much light a stimulus emits, while pattern concerns the arrangement of visual features within it.

The response rule remained unchanged: identical stimuli required remaining at the station, and different stimuli required approaching the monitor. The researchers interspersed the new brightness and pattern problems with shape problems. The animal thus applied the same action rule to different stimulus dimensions.

Performance reached approximately 77% correct on brightness problems and 80% on pattern problems. Correct responding occurred from the first presentation of the new relations. The animal used sameness and difference across variations in appearance that extended beyond the shapes used during acquisition.

figure.caption: Scholtyssek (2013), Fig. 6(a–b). Transfer to brightness and pattern relations.

slides.title: Motion coherence controls the strength of a visual signal
body: **Motion coherence** is the proportion of elements moving together in a common direction. Weiffen and colleagues presented random-dot displays to a harbour seal. At full coherence, all dots moved together; at lower coherence, directional dots were mixed with dots moving randomly.

The seal selected the display containing coherent upward motion in the initial task. Changing coherence altered the amount of directional information available while the same response earned reinforcement. The investigators also manipulated dot density and the duration for which individual dots remained visible.

The seal detected coherent motion when only a minority of dots supplied the common direction. Across the tested conditions, thresholds ranged from approximately 5% to 35% coherence. A population of moving elements therefore supported a directional choice even when many individual dot movements differed from the rewarded direction.

figure.caption: Weiffen (2014), Fig. 1. Published random-dot stimuli varying in motion coherence.

refs: Weiffen Michael, Mauck Björn, Dehnhardt Guido, Hanke Frederike D (2014). Sensitivity of a harbor seal (Phoca vitulina) to coherent visual motion in random dot displays. SpringerPlus 3(1):688. https://doi.org/10.1186/2193-1801-3-688

Changing coherence altered the amount of directional information available while the same response earned reinforcement. The investigators also manipulated dot density and the duration for which individual dots remained visible.

slides.title: Short dot lifetimes emphasize motion across the display
body: A dot’s **lifetime** is the interval for which that individual element remains visible before replacement. In Weiffen and colleagues’ experiment, shortening dot lifetime reduced the time available to follow any one dot. The seal still had to identify the display containing a common motion direction.

The published results compare coherence thresholds under different lifetimes and dot densities. Performance improved as the available motion information increased. Longer lifetimes supported lower coherence thresholds, while denser displays supplied more elements over the same visible area.

The seal also learned to discriminate opposite coherent-motion directions. Upward and downward motion provided different correct choices even though the displays shared their overall appearance. Directional information distributed across the changing dots guided the selected response.

figure.caption: Weiffen (2014), Fig. 3(a–e). Motion-coherence performance under different dot parameters.

slides.title: Underwater optic flow represents movement through space
body: **Optic flow** is the pattern of apparent image motion generated when an observer moves relative to the environment. Gläser and colleagues simulated forward travel through a cloud of dots on an underwater projection. The harbour seal viewed this moving pattern while holding its position at a hoop station.

The dots expanded outward from the simulated direction of travel. A reference cross was superimposed on the flow field, and the seal judged whether its location agreed with the apparent heading. Staying at the station or touching a response target reported the judgment.

The animal distinguished agreement from an offset between the reference and the flow-defined heading. The task linked the direction specified by many moving dots to a reinforced response. Underwater visual motion thus supplied information about simulated travel while the seal’s viewing position remained controlled.

figure.caption: Gläser (2014), Fig. 2(A–C). Underwater optic-flow apparatus and seal responses.

refs: Gläser Nele, Mauck Björn, Kandil Farid I., Lappe Markus, Dehnhardt Guido, Hanke Frederike D. (2014). Harbor Seals (Phoca vitulina) Can Perceive Optic Flow under Water. PLoS ONE 9(7):e103555. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0103555

slides.title: The focus of expansion specifies simulated heading
body: The **focus of expansion** is the point from which image elements appear to move outward during forward translation. In Gläser and colleagues’ underwater task, this point specified the simulated heading. Moving the reference cross away from it created a discrepancy for the seal to detect.

The researchers varied the angular distance between the reference and the focus of expansion. Detection improved as the offset increased. The published response function reached its halfway detection point at approximately **0.6°**, linking the animal’s judgment to a small change in visual direction.

The seal used the movement pattern to locate the heading even though the reference cross remained a separate visual element. Increasing their separation increased the evidence for a mismatch. The reinforced response depended on the spatial relationship between that reference and the heading specified by optic flow.

figure.caption: Gläser (2014), Fig. 3. Detecting offsets between the heading and reference cross.

slides.title: Surface optic flow retains information about heading
body: Sandow and colleagues presented harbour seals with three computer-generated motion environments: a cloud of dots filling a volume, a horizontal surface below the observer, and a horizontal surface above the observer. Each display simulated forward movement while the animal remained at a viewing station.

The simulated surfaces placed dots on a plane rather than throughout a volume. Their motion still specified a **heading**, the direction of travel. The seal reported whether that direction lay to the left or right using separate response targets positioned beside the monitor.

The seals learned heading judgments for both surface arrangements. The common choice requirement extended across displays with different spatial distributions of dots. The uploaded Luca recording adds visible task context: the animal watches moving dots and then contacts a side response target.

figure.caption: Sandow (2025), Fig. 1(A–D). Viewing chamber and volume, above-surface and below-surface optic flow.

refs: Sandow Laura-Marie, Thimian Ann-Kathrin, Lappe Markus, Hanke Frederike D. (2025). Optic flow, a rich source of optic information for harbour seals ( Phoca vitulina ). Journal of Experimental Biology 228(10):jeb250168. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.250168

slides.title: Heading precision persists across optic-flow geometry
body: Sandow and colleagues measured a **heading accuracy threshold**, the angular deviation associated with the task’s defined performance level. After task acquisition, the seals judged whether simulated movement deviated left or right. The experiment retained the same response alternatives across the three optic-flow environments.

Mean thresholds were approximately **4.61°** for volume flow, **4.96°** for flow from a surface below the observer, and **3.58°** for flow from a surface above the observer. These measures connect the strength of the directional judgment with the simulated geometry.

The seals acquired the task at different rates, then performed accurate directional judgments with each environment. The motion pattern supplied a heading from either a distributed cloud or a planar surface. Changing where the visible elements lay in space preserved information usable for the left–right response.

figure.caption: Sandow (2025), Fig. 2(A–C). Acquisition of heading judgments for surface optic flow.

refs: Sandow Laura-Marie, Thimian Ann-Kathrin, Lappe Markus, Hanke Frederike D. (2025). Optic flow, a rich source of optic information for harbour seals ( Phoca vitulina ). Journal of Experimental Biology 228(10):jeb250168. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.250168

slides.title: Target detection depends on the angle an object subtends
body: **Single-target acuity** is the smallest angular size at which an isolated target can be detected. Sandow, Miersch and Hanke measured underwater detection of dark dots displayed against a lighter background. A harbour seal placed its head at a station and selected a response target indicating the display condition.

**Visual angle** specifies the size of an object at the eye and depends on its physical size and viewing distance. The apparatus fixed the viewing arrangement while dot size was varied. This allowed the detection threshold to be expressed in degrees rather than only in millimetres on the screen.

For the seal Nick, high-contrast underwater thresholds were approximately **0.30°** for stationary dots and **0.27°** for moving dots. The same task connected visibility of a compact object with a reinforced choice. Movement and target size were manipulated within a controlled viewing preparation.

figure.caption: Sandow (2026), Fig. 1(a–c). Underwater target-acuity preparation and seal response.

refs: Sandow Laura-Marie, Miersch Lars, Hanke Frederike D. (2026). Underwater visual single target acuity in harbor seals (Phoca vitulina). Journal of Comparative Physiology A :advance online publication, 20 August 2026. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00359-026-01837-x

**Visual angle** specifies the size of an object at the eye and depends on its physical size and viewing distance. The apparatus fixed the viewing arrangement while dot size was varied. This allowed the detection threshold to be expressed in degrees rather than only in millimetres on the screen.

slides.title: Lower contrast increases the detectable target size
body: **Contrast** describes the difference between a target and its background. Sandow and colleagues varied the contrast of the dot while measuring underwater single-target acuity. The target remained compact, and the seal used the same response arrangement to report its presence.

At high contrast, Nick detected stationary dots subtending approximately **0.30°**. At the lowest contrast tested, the stationary threshold increased to approximately **0.63°**. A weaker luminance difference therefore required a larger angular target to support the reinforced judgment.

The published comparison includes both stationary and moving targets under the contrast conditions. Both sets of thresholds increased as contrast weakened. The relationship links the visual difference available at the eye with the size of the object that the animal could detect.

figure.caption: Sandow (2026), Fig. 2. Target acuity at different published Weber contrasts.

slides.title: A timed visual stimulus can determine the rewarded choice
body: Heinrich and colleagues trained a harbour seal to discriminate the duration of a white circle presented on a black monitor. **Interval discrimination** requires judging how long an event lasts. The animal selected one of two response targets after the circle disappeared.

A **standard interval** was compared with a longer interval. The appearance of the circle was retained while its duration changed, so elapsed time determined the correct response. Chamber illumination was controlled at **40 lx**, providing a stable viewing environment for the timing judgments.

The seal learned to select the response associated with the standard or longer duration. The event’s onset and offset supplied the temporal boundaries of the problem. Correct choices linked the interval between those boundaries to reinforcement delivered after the response.

figure.caption: Heinrich (2016), Fig. 1. Display and response targets for interval discrimination.

refs: Heinrich Tamara, Dehnhardt Guido, Hanke Frederike D. (2016). Harbour seals (Phoca vitulina) are able to time precisely. Animal Cognition 19(6):1133-1142. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10071-016-1020-3

slides.title: Longer intervals require larger temporal differences
body: A **difference threshold** is the smallest change in a stimulus that supports the task’s specified discrimination performance. Heinrich and colleagues varied the longer comparison interval around a standard duration. The seal reported the interval category through its response-target choice.

The experiment tested standard intervals from **3 s to 30 s**. Difference thresholds increased as the standard became longer. Across that range, the animal discriminated changes corresponding to roughly **15%** of the standard interval, expressing a similar relative timing sensitivity.

This pattern follows **Weber’s law**, in which a detectable difference scales with the magnitude of the reference stimulus. Longer reference durations supported larger absolute thresholds while the relative change remained comparable. The seal’s timing judgments retained that proportional relationship across the tested intervals.

figure.caption: Heinrich (2016), Fig. 4. Difference thresholds increase with the standard interval.

refs: Heinrich Tamara, Dehnhardt Guido, Hanke Frederike D. (2016). Harbour seals (Phoca vitulina) are able to time precisely. Animal Cognition 19(6):1133-1142. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10071-016-1020-3

slides.title: Fur seals and harbour seals share relative timing sensitivity
body: Heinrich, Ravignani and Hanke compared interval discrimination in a South African fur seal and a harbour seal. The fur seal belongs to the same otariid family as sea lions. Both animals judged how long a white circle remained visible on a black monitor.

Across much of the tested range, difference thresholds scaled with the standard duration. Relative thresholds averaged approximately **12%** in the fur seal and **14%** in the harbour seal. The proportional range extended from about **0.8–7 s** in the fur seal and **0.8–30 s** in the harbour seal.

At very short intervals, relative thresholds increased, separating that regime from the approximately proportional timing range. The same display and response structure exposed this change in sensitivity. Duration supplied information for a reinforced choice in both an otariid and a phocid seal.

figure.caption: Heinrich (2020), Fig. 2(a–d). Relative interval-discrimination thresholds in fur seal and harbour seal.

refs: Heinrich Tamara, Ravignani Andrea, Hanke Frederike D. (2020). Visual timing abilities of a harbour seal (Phoca vitulina) and a South African fur seal (Arctocephalus pusillus pusillus) for sub- and supra-second time intervals. Animal Cognition 23(5):851-859. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10071-020-01390-3

slides.title: Landmarks specify a goal through distance and direction
body: A **landmark** is a conspicuous environmental feature that can support orientation to a place. Maaß and Hanke trained harbour seals to touch an unmarked goal within an array of illuminated landmarks on a submerged panel. The illuminated points defined the spatial context for locating the goal.

The panel contained a grid of LEDs spaced **15 cm** apart. The landmark array was presented at different panel positions, while the goal retained its trained relationship to the landmarks. Correct snout contact at the goal produced reinforcement.

In the expanded arrays, the seals mainly searched at locations consistent with a **directional vector**, a remembered distance and direction from a landmark. The responses retained learned goal–landmark relationships as the surrounding arrangement changed. Distances and directions provided a spatial basis for the reinforced search.

figure.caption: Maaß (2022), Fig. 3(A–E). Baseline and expanded landmark arrays.

refs: Maaß Eric, Hanke Frederike D. (2022). How harbour seals ( Phoca vitulina ) encode goals relative to landmarks. Journal of Experimental Biology 225(5):jeb243870. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.243870
transcript: A **landmark** is a conspicuous environmental feature that can support orientation to a place. Maaß and Hanke trained harbour seals to touch an unmarked goal within an array of illuminated landmarks on a submerged panel. The illuminated points defined the spatial context for locating the goal.

The panel contained a grid of LEDs spaced **15 cm** apart. The landmark array was presented at different panel positions, while the goal retained its trained relationship to the landmarks. Correct snout contact at the goal produced reinforcement.

In the expanded arrays, the seals mainly searched at locations consistent with a **directional vector**, a remembered distance and direction from a landmark. The responses retained learned goal–landmark relationships as the surrounding arrangement changed. Distances and directions provided a spatial basis for the reinforced search.

slides.title: Array expansion separates spatial search strategies
body: Maaß and Hanke expanded trained landmark arrays horizontally, vertically or diagonally. These changes moved the landmarks apart while retaining recognizable points. The seal’s response location was recorded on the LED grid after it viewed the altered arrangement.

A **beacon strategy** targets a conspicuous marker itself, while a directional-vector strategy targets an offset from that marker. A **geometric rule** uses a relation within the arrangement, such as its center. Expanding the array created different predicted search locations for these strategies.

The recorded responses were concentrated near positions compatible with learned directional offsets. When fewer landmarks defined the array, some animals changed their search pattern. The spatial configuration affected which learned relationship governed the location selected for a response.

figure.caption: Maaß (2022), Fig. 4(A–C). Search locations after expansion of a four-landmark array.

slides.title: Midpoint training varies landmark spacing and orientation
body: Maaß and colleagues trained the harbour seal Moe to respond halfway between two illuminated landmarks. A **midpoint** lies at equal distance from the two endpoints. The goal was unlit, requiring the seal to locate it from the landmark arrangement rather than contact a visible goal marker.

Training introduced vertical and horizontal arrays with different inter-landmark distances. Configurations labeled **3LEDv** and **5LEDv** had landmark separations of **60 cm** and **90 cm**, respectively. These labels describe the intervening grid positions, not the number of illuminated landmarks.

Moe learned midpoint responses as training varied spacing and orientation. The midpoint changed its panel location with the landmark pair, while the equal-distance relation remained the rewarded rule. Reinforcement selected a spatial relationship that could be applied across several familiar configurations.

figure.caption: Maaß (2022), Fig. 1(A–B). Landmark configurations and Moe’s midpoint response.

refs: Maaß Eric, Miersch Lars, Pfuhl Gerit, Hanke Frederike D. (2022). A harbour seal ( Phoca vitulina ) can learn geometrical relationships between landmarks. Journal of Experimental Biology 225(24):jeb244544. https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.244544

slides.title: Novel landmark separations retain the midpoint goal
body: After midpoint training, Maaß and colleagues presented unfamiliar landmark arrangements to Moe. Some had smaller or larger separations than those used during acquisition, and others rotated familiar configurations. The animal still had to select the unmarked position halfway between the illuminated endpoints.

Test arrays included separations of **30 cm** and **150 cm**, extending beyond the distances used during the initial training stages. The seal responded at the midpoint on its first trials with the new configurations. Responses retained the equal-distance relationship across the changed geometry.

During transfer sessions, familiar baseline arrays continued to reward midpoint responses. Moe selected the midpoint in **89%** of these baseline trials. Interleaving familiar and novel configurations maintained the trained response during testing, while changes in landmark separation moved the goal without changing its equal-distance relation to both endpoints.

slides.title: Southern sea lions use changing urban resting habitats
body: Rodríguez and colleagues examined male southern sea-lion aggregations in the Argentine fishing harbors of Mar del Plata and Quequén. The animals used human-built resting sites, including docks, breakwaters and vessel decks. These sites offered access to resting space alongside active port operations.

The chapter describes changes in harbor use across decades and connections with breeding grounds approximately **700 km** away. Males dispersed seasonally and returned to harbor resting areas. **Site fidelity**, repeated use of a location, linked these urban habitats with the animals’ broader annual movements.

The sea lions used fish offal together with natural foraging and shifted resting locations as port conditions changed. Their recurring use of particular areas combined with changes in local occupation. The observations connect learned use of human environments with seasonal movement and access to food.

slides.title: New Zealand sea lions combine fidelity with dispersal
body: Chilvers describes strong **philopatry**, a tendency to return to the place of birth, in New Zealand sea lions. Repeated use of breeding colonies concentrates reproduction in familiar locations. The species also includes females that establish breeding sites far from their natal colonies.

Some females dispersed more than **700 km** before breeding in new areas. The chapter links recolonization with differences in breeding-site use, including vegetation and inland locations. These choices alter the physical and social conditions encountered by mothers and pups.

Breeding females used scrub and other terrestrial habitats for pupping and shelter. At established and recolonized sites, movements between coastal access points and breeding areas connected marine foraging with terrestrial care of offspring. Site fidelity and dispersal produced different patterns of repeated habitat use within the same species.

slides.title: Otariid sensory access changes between air and water
body: Hanke, Reichmuth and Cook describe the sensory adaptations of sea lions and fur seals living in air and water. Otariids have large eyes, an external ear and **vibrissae**, facial sensory hairs used in mechanoreception. These structures collect information during both terrestrial and aquatic behavior.

The chapter describes an eye with a flattened central corneal region and a flexible pupil. These features contribute to viewing across the different optical properties of air and water. The retina is dominated by light-sensitive rods, supporting vision under dim conditions encountered during aquatic activity.

The external ear, or pinna, is visible on the head, while the nostrils close during underwater travel. The eyes and vibrissae collect visual and mechanical information. Returning to land changes the physical medium through which visual, acoustic and tactile information arrives. Otariid behavior coordinates those sensory inputs with movement, foraging and recognition of other animals.

figure.caption: Hanke (2021), Fig. 16.1(a–c). California sea lion, eye and external ear.

items.text: Identity and same/different tasks reinforce relationships among stimuli; transfer tests evaluate use of those relationships with new materials.
Coherent dot motion and optic flow provide information about direction, while dot lifetime, density and spatial geometry change the available signal.
Single-target acuity depends on angular size and contrast; lower contrast requires larger targets for reliable detection.
Harbour seals and fur seals use stimulus duration to guide reinforced choices, with approximately proportional sensitivity over substantial timing ranges.
Directional vectors and midpoint rules specify different goal locations when landmarks move or change their spacing.
Sea-lion sensory systems and recurring habitat use connect aquatic foraging, terrestrial breeding and interaction with human environments.
